# DISCRETE GROUPS GENERATED BY REFLECTIONS IN LOBAČEVSKÍÍ SPACES

E. B. VINBERG\*

UDC 519.45

# Introduction

It is well known that in Euclidean space discrete groups generated by reflections are specified by nonnegative symmetrical matrices $A = (a_{ij})$, where $a_{ii} = 1$, $a_{ij} = -\cos \pi / m_{ij}$ ($i \neq j$), and the $m_{ij}$ can assume the values 2, 3, $\dots$, $\infty$. A complete enumeration of these matrices was given by Coxeter [1].

In the first part of the present paper we shall prove (Theorem 1) that in Lobačevskii space the discrete groups generated by finitely many reflections and having a finite fundamental region can be described with the aid of symmetric matrices of negative inertial index 1 that have $a_{ii} = 1$, $a_{ij} = -\cos \pi / m_{ij}$ or $a_{ij} &lt; -1$ and contain sufficiently many (in a certain sense) submatrices of Coxeter type. This provides us with an effective means for constructing such groups.

In the second part of the paper we ascertain those among the above-mentioned groups that are arithmetical in the sense of Borel and Harish-Chandra [2]. It is found (Theorem 2) that the necessary and sufficient conditions for such groups are as follows: The numbers $2a_{ij}$ must be completely real algebraic integers, and the matrix $A$ must be nonnegative for all morphisms in $C$, i.e. morphisms of the field generated by the $2a_{ij}$, that are not the identity on a subfield generated by numbers of the form $a_{i_1 i_2} a_{i_2 i_3} \cdots a_{i_m i_1}$.

In the third part we present various examples of discrete groups generated by reflections in Lobačevskii spaces. Thus we construct examples of nonarithmetic groups with a fundamental region of finite volume in the dimensionalities 3, 4, 5, and with a compact fundamental region in the dimensionalities 3 and 4.

# I. GEOMETRICAL PART

## 1. The fundamental polyhedron of a discrete group, generated by reflections

Let $S$ be either an $n$-dimensional Euclidean space $E^n$ or an $n$-dimensional Lobachevskii space $\Lambda^n$. A convex polyhedron in $S$ is defined as the intersection of finitely many closed halfspaces that contains a nonempty open set, and a reflection denotes a reflection in a hyperplane.

Let $\Gamma$ be a discrete group of motions of the space $S$ that is generated by finitely many reflections. The hyperplanes of all reflections contained in $\Gamma$ decompose $S$ into convex polyhedra, called $\Gamma$-cells. Each of these cells is a fundamental region for $\Gamma$, and the reflections at its edges generate a group $\Gamma$. It is also known that a convex polyhedron $P$ is a $\Gamma$-cell for some group $\Gamma$ of the type under con

$(R)$  All the dihedral angles of  $P$  are submultiples of  $\pi$ .
$(R^{\prime})$  All the angles between the hyperplanes, bounding  $P$ , are submultiples of  $\pi$ .

# $\frac{\partial}{\partial 2}$  C-polyhedra in Euclidean space

We shall describe a convex polyhedron  $P \subset E^n$  with the aid of unit vectors  $e_i$  that are perpendicular to the hyperplanes  $H_i$  bounding  $P$  and are directed away from  $P$ . The Gram matrix  $A = (a_{ij})$  of the system of vectors  $e_i$  will be called the Gram matrix of the polyhedron  $P$ . If the hyperplanes  $H_i$  and  $H_j$  form an angle  $\alpha$ , then

$$
a _ {i j} = \left(e _ {i}, e _ {j}\right) = - \cos \alpha ; \tag {1}
$$

if these hyperplanes are parallel, then

$$
a _ {i j} = \left(e _ {i}, e _ {j}\right) = - 1. \tag {2}
$$

A polyhedron  $P$  is said to be decomposable if the space  $E$  can be decomposed into a direct product  $E_1 \times \dots \times E_k$  of Euclidean spaces  $E_i$  in such a way that  $P = P_1 \times \dots \times P_k$ , where  $P_i$  is a convex polyhedron in  $E_i$ . The Gram matrix  $A$  of  $P$  is in this case the direct sum of the Gram matrices  $A_i$  of the polyhedra  $P_i$ :

$$
A = A _ {1} \oplus \dots \oplus A _ {k} = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} A _ {1} &amp; &amp; \\ 0 &amp; \ddots &amp; \\ &amp; &amp; A _ {k} \end{array} \right). \tag {3}
$$

A polyhedron  $P$  is said to be a  $C$ -polyhedron if all the angles formed by its bounding hyperplanes do not exceed  $90^\circ$  and if it does not contain any straight line.

The Gram matrix  $A$  of a  $C$ -polyhedron in  $E^n$  is a nonnegative symmetric matrix of rank  $n$ , with

$$
a _ {i i} = 1, \quad a _ {i j} \leqslant 0 (i \neq j). \tag {4}
$$

Such matrices will be called  $C$ -matrices.

It is well known [1] that there are two sorts of  $C$ -matrices of rank  $n$ , nondecomposable into a direct sum.

1. Nondecomposable  $C^*$ -matrices, which are positive matrices of order  $n$ . Each such matrix is the Gram matrix of a unique convex polyhedron in  $E^n$  which is a simplicial angle. All the elements of the inverse matrix are positive.
2. Nondecomposable  $C^0$ -matrices, which are nonnegative matrices of order  $n + 1$ . Each such matrix is the Gram matrix of a unique (to within similitude) convex polyhedron in  $E^n$  which is a simplex. All the principal submatrices* of order  $n$  are positive. The rows are linearly dependent with positive coefficients.

DISCRETE GROUPS

It follows from the classification of nondecomposable $C$-matrices that any $C$-polyhedron $P$ can be decomposed into a direct product of a simplicial angle and of several simplexes. If $P$ is a polyhedral angle, it will be a simplicial angle. If $P$ is bounded, it will be a direct product of simplexes. The Gram matrices of these two types of $C$-polyhedra will be called $C^+$- and $C^0$-matrices respectively. It is clear that $C^+$-matrices ($C^0$-matrices) are $C$-matrices which can be decomposed into a direct sum of nondecomposable $C^+$-matrices (nondecomposable $C^0$-matrices).

Let $P \subset E^n$ be a $C$-polyhedron, $A$ its Gram matrix, and $F$ its face. Let us consider those $e_i$ vectors that are orthogonal to $F$. The Gram matrix of this vector system, regarded as a submatrix of $A$, will be denoted by $A(F)$. It is easy to see that the mapping $F \to A(F)$ is a one-to-one mapping of the set of all faces of the polyhedron $P$ (different from the polyhedron itself) onto the set of all principal $C^+$-submatrices of $A$, with

$$
\dim F = n \text{ (the rank of } A(F) \text{)} \tag{5}
$$

$$
F_1 \subset F_2 \Leftrightarrow A(F_1) \supset A(F_2). \tag{6}
$$

## §3. $C^-$-polyhedra in Lobačevski space

Let $E^{n,1}$ be an $(n + 1)$-dimensional vector space over $\mathbf{R}$, endowed with a nondegenerate scalar product of negative inertial index 1. Let us consider the set

$$
V = \{x \in E^{n,1} : (x, x) &lt; 0\}. \tag{7}
$$

It consists of two connected components, say $V_+$ and $V_-$. The points of the $n$-dimensional Lobačevskii space $\Lambda^n$ will be identified with the rays (emergent from the origin) in $E^{n,1}$ that lie in a cone $V_+$. The motions of the space $\Lambda^n$ in this model will be the mappings induced by the automorphisms of the space $E^{n,1}$ that leave $V_+$ invariant.

A subspace of $E^{n,1}$ is said to be hyperbolic (elliptic, parabolic) if the scalar product induced on it is nondegenerate and indefinite (positive, degenerate). The orthogonal complement of a hyperbolic (elliptic, parabolic) subspace is an elliptic (hyperbolic, parabolic) subspace of complementary dimensionality.

To every $s$-dimensional plane $\Pi \subset \Lambda^n$ corresponds an $(s + 1)$-dimensional hyperbolic subspace in $E^{n,1}$ that will be denoted by $\widehat{\Pi}$. To every halfspace in $\Lambda^n$ corresponds a halfspace in $E^{n,1}$, bounded by a hyperbolic hypersubspace. By definition, a convex polyhedron $P \subset \Lambda^n$ is the intersection of several halfspaces. The intersection of the corresponding halfspaces in $E^{n,1}$ will be denoted by $\widehat{P}$. It will be in the form of a polyhedral angle with vertex at the origin; we shall stipulate that the origin does not belong to it. The polyhedron $P$ can be unambiguously determined from $\widehat{P}$ as being the totality of rays lying in $\widehat{P} \cap V_+$. For the polyhedron $P$ to be bounded in $\Lambda^n$ it is necessary and sufficient that

$$
\widehat{P} \subset V_+; \tag{8}
$$

the necessary and sufficient condition for $P$ to have a finite volume is

$$
\widehat{P} \subset \overline{V}_+. \tag{9}
$$

In the latter case only some of the ribs of the angle $\widehat{P}$ belong to the boundary of the cone $V_+$; we shall stipulate that to them correspond "infinitely distant" vertices of $P$.

Let us consider in $E^{n,1}$ vectors $e_i$ that are perpendicular to the hyperplanes $\widehat{H}_i$ of the $n$-dimen

É. B. VINBERG

sional faces of the angle $\hat{P}$ and are directed away from $\hat{P}$. These vectors will be normalized by the condition

$$
(e_i, e_i) = 1. \tag{10}
$$

This can be done, since the subspaces $\hat{H}_i$ are hyperbolic and hence $(e_i, e_i) &gt; 0$.

The angle $\hat{P}$ is determined by the inequalities

$$
(e_i, x) \leqslant 0. \tag{11}
$$

Since $\dim \hat{P} = n + 1$, it follows that none of these inequalities goes over into an equality everywhere on $\hat{P}$. Therefore the vectors $e_i$ cannot be related by a linear dependence with nonnegative coefficients.

The Gram matrix $A = (a_{ij})$ of the system of vectors $e_i$ will be called the Gram matrix of the polyhedron $P$. If the hyperplanes $H_i$ and $H_j$ of two faces of $P$ form an angle $\alpha$, then

$$
a_{ij} = (e_i, e_j) = -\cos \alpha; \tag{12}
$$

if they intersect, then

$$
a_{ij} = (e_i, e_j) \leqslant -1. \tag{13}
$$

In order to prove the latter assertion we let $H_i$ and $H_j$ coincide by a continuous motion in such a way that they do not intersect throughout the motion. Then $|(e_i, e_j)|$ will be smaller than 1 throughout; but it is evident that at the end of the motion we have $e_i = -e_j$ and $(e_i, e_j) = -1$.

If the rank of the matrix $A$ is equal to $n + 1$, it will specify the vectors $e_i$, and hence also the angle $\hat{P}$, to within an automorphism of the space $E^{n+1}$. In order to determine the polyhedron $P$ from the matrix $A$, we must know which of the connected components of the set $V$ should be taken as $V_*. If (9) is satisfied, this question will evidently have an unambiguous answer.

**Lemma 1.** If condition (9) is satisfied, the rank of the matrix $A$ will be $n + 1$.

Indeed, if the rank of $A$ were smaller than $n + 1$, the rank of the vector system $e_i$ would also be smaller than $n + 1$, and the angle $\hat{P}$, defined by (11), would contain a straight line. It is clear that this is incompatible with (9).

**Definition.** A convex polyhedron $P \subset \Lambda^n$ is said to be a $C^\infty$-polyhedron if it has a finite volume and if all the angles between its bounding hyperplanes do not exceed $90^\circ$.

From (12) and (13) it follows that all nondiagonal elements of the Gram matrix of a $C^\infty$-polyhedron are either negative or zero.

**Lemma 2.** The Gram matrix $A$ of a $C^\infty$-polyhedron $P$ is nondecomposable.

In fact, let $A = A_1 \oplus A_2$. One of the matrices $A_1$ and $A_2$ must be nonnegative. Suppose that $A_1$ is such a matrix, and let $e_1, \dots, e_k$ be vectors participating in the formation of $A_1$. Every linear dependence between rows of $A_1$ implies a similar dependence between vectors $e_1, \dots, e_k$. Hence there cannot be a linear dependence with nonnegative coefficients between the rows of $A_1$, so that $A_1$ is a $C^\infty$-matrix and the subspace $M$, generated by $e_1, \dots, e_k$, is an elliptic subspace. Every vector $x$ of $M$ that satisfies the inequalities $(e_i, x) \leq 0$ ($i = 1, \dots, k$), belongs to $\hat{P}$. This contradicts condition (9).

As in §2 we shall define a mapping $F \to A(F)$ of the set of faces of $P$ (including the infinitely distant vertices) into the set of principal submatrices of $A$.

Lemma 3. Let $P$ be a $C^*$-polyhedron and $F$ its $s$-dimensional ordinary face. Then $A(F)$ will be a $C^+$-matrix of rank $n - 1$. If $F$ is an infinitely distant vertex, then $A(F)$ will be a $C^0$-matrix of rank $n - 1$.

Let us denote by $\Pi$ the plane of the face $F$. The vectors $e_1, \dots, e_k$, participating in the formation of the matrix $A(F)$, generate a subspace $M$ which is the orthogonal complement of $\Pi$. If $F$ is an $s$-dimensional ordinary face, then $M$ will be an $(n - s)$-dimensional elliptic subspace; if $F$ is an infinitely distant vertex, then $M$ will be an $n$-dimensional parabolic subspace. The matrix $A(F)$ is nonnegative in either case.

If $M$ is an elliptic subspace, every linear dependence between the rows of the matrix $A(F)$ will imply a similar dependence between the vectors $e_1, \dots, e_k$. Hence there cannot be a linear dependence with nonnegative coefficients between the rows of $A(F)$, so that $A(F)$ is a $C^+$-matrix.

It still remains to prove that if $F$ is an infinitely distant vertex, then $A(F)$ will be a $C^0$-matrix. Let us assume that $A(F) = A_1 \oplus A_2$, where $A_1$ is a $C^+$-matrix. Let $e_1, \dots, e_l$ ($l \leq k$) be vectors participating in the formation of $A_1$. The subspace $M_1$ generated by these vectors is elliptic. Let us take some nonzero vector $x$ of $M_1$ that satisfies the inequalities $(e_i, x) \leq 0$ ($i = 1, \dots, l$). If $f \in \widehat{\Pi} \cap \overline{V}_+$, then $f + \epsilon x \in \widehat{P}$ for all sufficiently small $\epsilon$; but this contradicts condition (9), since $(f + \epsilon x, f + \epsilon x) = \epsilon^2(x, x) &gt; 0$. The lemma is proved.

Let us now consider an arbitrary symmetric matrix $A$ that satisfies the following conditions.

(L1) The rank of $A$ is $n + 1$, the negative inertial index being equal to 1.
(L2) $a_{ii} = 1$, $a_{ij} \leq 0$ ($i \neq j$).
(L3) The matrix $A$ is nondecomposable.

It follows from (L1) that $A$ is Gram's matrix of some vector system $e_i \in E^{n,1}$. Let us denote by $\hat{P}$ the convex set defined by (11).

Lemma 4. With appropriately selected notations for the connected components of the cone $V$, we have:

1) $\hat{P} \cap V_{+}$ contains a nonempty open set.
2) $\hat{P} \cap \overline{V}_{-} = \emptyset$.
3) If $B$ is the maximal positive principal submatrix of $A, e_1, \dots, e_k$ the vectors related to it, and $N$ the orthogonal complement of the subspace $M$ spanned by $e_1, \dots, e_k$, then $\hat{P} \supset N \cap \overline{V}$.
4) For $i &gt; k$ the inequalities (11) are strictly satisfied on the set $N \cap V_{+}$.

First let us prove assertion 3. We shall denote by $f_{i}$ ($i &gt; k$) the orthogonal projection of the vector $e_{i}$ on $N$. If

$$
A = \left( \begin{array}{cc} B &amp; C \\ C' &amp; D \end{array} \right),
$$

then Gram's matrix for the vectors $f_i$ will be the matrix $D_1 = D - C'B^{-1}C$. Since all the elements of $B^{-1}$ are nonnegative, it follows that all nondiagonal elements of $D_1$ are negative or zero. Similarly, none of the diagonal elements of $D_1$ can be positive, since otherwise the matrix $B$ would not be a maximal positive principal submatrix. Therefore all the vectors $f_i$ will lie in the closure of one half of the cone $V$; let us denote it by $V_+$.

The set $\hat{P} \cap N$ is assigned in $N$ by the inequalities $(f_i, x) \leq 0$, and hence it contains $N \cap \overline{V}_+$.

The vectors $f_i$ generate $N$. Hence there exist nonnegative numbers $c_i$ such that $f = \sum c_i f_i \in V_+$. Since the $f_i$ can be expressed in terms of $e_j$ with nonnegative coefficients, it follows that $(f, x) \leq 0$ for all $x \in \tilde{P}$. On the other hand, since $f \in V_+$, it follows that $(f, x) &gt; 0$ for $x \in \tilde{V}_-$. This proves assertion 2 of the lemma.

In order to prove assertion 4 we shall assume that $(e_{k+1}, x) = 0$ for some $x \in N \cap V_+$. Then $(e_{k+1}, x) = 0$ for all $x \in N$, and hence $e_{k+1}$ can be expressed linearly in terms of $e_1, \dots, e_k$. Gram’s matrix of the vectors $e_1, \dots, e_k$, $e_{k+1}$ is a $C$-matrix of rank $k$; therefore the coefficients of any linear dependence between $e_1, \dots, e_k$, $e_{k+1}$ must have the same sign. Let us assume that

$$
\sum_{i = l + 1}^{k + 1} b_i e_i = 0, \quad b_i &gt; 0.
$$

Then $a_{ij} = 0$ for $l &lt; i \leq k + 1$ and $j \leq l$ or $j &gt; k + 1$, and the matrix $A$ is decomposable, which contradicts condition (L3).

Finally let us prove assertion 1 of the lemma. By $Q$ we shall denote the set formed by vectors of type $x + y$, where $x \in N$, $y \in M$, $(e_i, y) &lt; 0$ for $i = 1, \dots, k$. Let $x_0$ be a point of $N \cap V_+$, and $U$ be a neighborhood of this point that is contained in $V_+$ and on which we have $(e_i, x) &lt; 0$ for $i &gt; k$. Then the set $Q \cap U$ will be nonempty, open and contained in $\tilde{P} \cap V_+$. This completes the proof of the lemma.

Now let us denote by $P$ a set of rays contained in $\tilde{P} \cap V_+$. From assertion 1 of Lemma 4 it follows that $P$ is a convex polyhedron in $\Lambda^n$.

The mapping $F \to A(F)$ will be determined in a similar way, as though the matrix $A$ were the Gram matrix of $P$ (we shall see below that this is indeed the case).

**Lemma 5.** Let $A_1$ be a principal $C^+$-submatrix of rank $n - s$ of $A$. Then $A_1 = A(F)$, where $F$ is an $s$-dimensional ordinary face of $P$. If $A_1$ is a principal $C^0$-submatrix of rank $n - 1$, then $A_1 = A(F)$, where $F$ is an infinitely distant vertex.

The first part of the lemma can be easily obtained from assertions 3 and 4 of Lemma 4 by including $A_1$ in the maximal principal $C^+$-submatrix $B$ and using the same construction as in the proof of assertion 1 of Lemma 4.

Let us prove the second part of the lemma. Suppose that $A_1$ is a $C^0$-matrix of rank $n - 1$, and $e_1, \dots, e_k$ are vectors participating in its formation. The vectors $e_1, \dots, e_k$ cannot be related by a linear dependence with nonnegative coefficients, since otherwise the matrix $A$ would be decomposable (see the proof of assertion 4 of Lemma 4). Hence the subspace $M$ spanned by these vectors is an $n$-dimensional parabolic subspace. The orthogonal complement of $M$ is one-dimensional and it is generated by an isotropic vector $e$ that can be represented as $e = \sum_{i=1}^{k} c_i e_i$, where all the $c_i$ are positive. It is clear that $(e_j, e) \leq 0$ for $j &gt; k$, and the equality $(e_j, e) = 0$ implies $(e_j, e_i) = 0$ for all $i \leq k$, and hence $e_j = \lambda e$, which is impossible, since $(e_j, e_j) = 1$. This implies the assertion of the lemma.

From Lemma 5 it follows, in particular, that the matrix $A$ is Gram’s matrix of the polyhedron $P$. As a matter of fact, let us apply the lemma to a submatrix $A_1$ consisting of a single element $a_{ii}$. We then find that the equation $(e_i, x)$ specifies the $(n - 1)$-dimensional face of $P$ and that no other vector $e_j$ is orthogonal to the hypersubspace $\tilde{H}_i$ corresponding to this face. Thus there are no redundant $e_i$-vectors. Since the angle $\tilde{P}$ is specified by (11), the vectors $e_i$ are directed away from $\tilde{P}$.

**Theorem 1.** In order that a symmetric matrix $A = (a_{ij})$ should be the Gram matrix of a $C^-$-poly-

hedron $P$ of the space $\Lambda^n$, it is necessary and sufficient that it satisfy the conditions (L1)-(L3) and the following conditions:

(L4) $A$ has at least one principal submatrix which is either a $C^+$-matrix of rank $n$ or a $C^0$-matrix of rank $n - 1$; such matrices are called nodal matrices.

(L5) For every nodal submatrix $B_1$ and any of its $C^+$-submatrices $B$ of rank $n - 1$ there exists a nodal submatrix $B_2$ containing $B$ and distinct from $B_1$.

Proof. Let $A$ be a symmetric matrix that satisfies conditions (L1)-(L5). It then follows from Lemmas 4 and 5 that $A$ is Gram's matrix of a convex polyhedron $P \subset \Lambda^n$, with the vertices of $P$ corresponding to the nodal submatrices and the edges of $P$ corresponding to $C^+$-submatrices of rank $n - 1$. Property (L4) signifies that $P$ has vertices, and property (L5) signifies that any edge of $P$ that originates at any of the vertices is incident with another vertex. It is easy to see that this yields (9). Using also (12), we find that $P$ is a $C^+$-polyhedron.

The necessity of conditions (L1)-(L5) follows from relations (10), (12) and (13) and Lemmas 1, 2, 3 and 5.

Symmetric matrices $A$ that satisfy conditions (L1)-(L5) will be called $C^-$-matrices.

## 4. Coxeter's diagrams

In order to find all the discrete groups of motions of Euclidean space generated by reflections, we must select those among the $C$-matrices (see $\frac{\partial}{\partial 2}$) whose nondiagonal elements have the form

$$
a_{ij} = -\cos \frac{\pi}{m_{ij}}, \tag{14}
$$

where the $m_{ij}$ can assume the values 2, 3, $\cdots$, $\infty$. This was done by Coxeter [1]. The diagrams proposed by him for the description of such matrices are constructed as follows. The number of vertices taken is equal to the order of the matrix, and the vertices $v_i$ and $v_j$ are joined by an $(m_{ij} - 2)$-tuple line or by a simple line with index $m_{ij}$.

In this notation, nondecomposable $C^+$-matrices which satisfy condition (14) can be described by the following diagrams (the subscripts indicate the rank of the matrix):

Similarly, in order to find all the discrete groups of motions of Lobačevskii space generated by finitely many reflections and having a finite fundamental region, we must select among all  $C^-$ -matrices (see §3) those with nondiagonal elements of the form

$$
a _ {i j} = - \cos \frac {\pi}{m _ {i j}} \quad \text {or} \quad a _ {i j} &lt;   - 1. \tag {15}
$$

The nodal submatrices of such  $C^-$ -matrices will be Coxeter-type matrices. For this reason the verification of conditions (L4) and (L5) does not require any calculations.

The description of  $C^-$ -matrices satisfying condition (15) can also be effected with the aid of Coxeter's diagrams, with the additional stipulation that in the case  $a_{ij} &lt; -1$  the vertices  $v_i$  and  $v_j$  are joined by a dotted line on which we indicate (if desired) the number  $-a_{ij}$ .

## II. ALGEBRAIC PART

## §5. Arithmetic groups

There exists one general method of construction of discrete subgroups  $\Gamma$  of a semisimple Lie group  $\mathfrak{G}$  for which the volume of the factor space  $\mathfrak{G} / \Gamma$  is finite. This method, proposed by Borel and Harish-Chandra [2], will be described here in a form suitable for our purposes.

Let  $\mathfrak{G}$  be a Lie group with finitely many connected components, the connected component of unity  $\mathfrak{G}^0$  being the direct product of noncompact simple Lie groups without center. Furthermore, let  $G$  be an irreducible algebraic group, defined over the field of algebraic numbers  $\mathbf{K}$ . We shall assume that

DISCRETE GROUPS
437

(A1) the field $\mathbf{K}$ is completely real,
(A2) the group $G_{\mathbf{R}}$ is locally isomorphic to $\mathfrak{G}$,
(A3) for any nonidentity morphism $\sigma \colon \mathbf{K} \to \mathbf{R}$ the group $(G^{\sigma})_{\mathbf{R}}$ is compact.*

By selecting an exact matrix representation $\rho$ of $G$, we can consider the group

$$
G_{\mathrm{I}} = \{g \in G_{\mathrm{R}}: p(g)_{ij} \in \mathbf{I}\}, \tag{16}
$$

where $\mathbf{I}$ is the ring of integral elements of $\mathbf{K}$. It is well known that the group $G_{\mathbf{I}}$ does not depend on $\rho$ (to within commensurability). Let us denote by $\bar{\mathcal{Q}}(G, \mathbf{K})$ the class of subgroups of $\mathfrak{G}$ consisting of subgroups of the form $\phi(G_{\mathbf{I}})$, where $\phi$ is a homomorphism of $(G_{\mathbf{R}})^0$ on $\mathfrak{G}^0$, and of all subgroups commensurable with the latter.

The subgroups of $\mathfrak{G}$ which belong to $\mathbf{U}_{\mathbf{G},\mathbf{K}}\bar{\mathcal{Q}}(G,\mathbf{K})$ are called arithmetic subgroups. Any arithmetic subgroup $\Gamma \subset \mathfrak{G}$ is discrete; it follows from the results of [2] that the volume of the factor space $\mathfrak{G}/\Gamma$ is finite.

Let us also consider a class $Q\bar{\mathcal{Q}}(G, \mathbf{K})$ of discrete subgroups $\Gamma$ of $\mathfrak{G}$ such that the volume of $\mathfrak{G}/\Gamma$ is finite and some subgroup of finite index in $\Gamma$ is contained in $\phi(G_{\mathbf{K}})$, where $\phi$ is an appropriate homomorphism of $(G_{\mathbf{R}})^0$ on $\mathfrak{G}^0$. The subgroups belonging to $\mathbf{U}_{G,\mathbf{K}}Q\bar{\mathcal{Q}}(G, \mathbf{K})$ will be called quasi-arithmetic.

It is easy to see that

$$
\mathcal{A}(G, \mathbf{K}) = \mathcal{A}(\operatorname{Ad} G, \mathbf{K}), \tag{17}
$$

$$
Q\mathcal{A}(G, \mathbf{K}) \subset Q\mathcal{A}(\operatorname{Ad} G, \mathbf{K}), \tag{18}
$$

so that the store of arithmetic and quasi-arithmetic subgroups does not diminish if $G$ contains only groups without center.

In order to ascertain whether or not a quasi-arithmetic subgroup is arithmetical, we shall use the following lemma.

**Lemma 6.** Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over the field of algebraic numbers $\mathbf{K}$, $|u_i|$ a basis of $V$, $\mathbf{I}$ the ring of integers of the field $\mathbf{K}$, and $M(\mathbf{I})$ a set of matrices with elements in $\mathbf{I}$. The following properties of the group $\Gamma$ of linear transformations of the space $V$ are equivalent.

1) In $\Gamma$ there exists a subgroup $\Gamma_0$ of finite index, such that all its elements can be written in the basis $|u_i|$ with the aid of matrices belonging to $M(\mathbf{I})$.
2) There exists a natural number $m$ such that all the elements of $\Gamma$ can be written in the basis $|u_i|$ with the aid of matrices of the form $(1/m)A$, where $A \in M(\mathbf{I})$.
3) $\Gamma$ leaves invariant some $\mathbf{I}$-submodule $M \subset V$ of finite type, which generates over $\mathbf{K}$ all the space $V$.

**Proof.** 1) $\Rightarrow$ 2). Let $\Gamma = \mathbf{U}_{k=1}^{s} \gamma_{k} \Gamma_{0}$ and suppose that $\gamma_{k}$ can be written in the basis $|u_{i}|$ with the aid of the matrix $(1/m_{k})A_{k}$, where $A_{k} \in M(\mathbf{I})$. It is clear that $m$ can be taken in the form of a common multiple of the numbers $m_{k}$.

2) $\Rightarrow$ 3). We shall take $M$ in the form of an $\mathbf{I}$-submodule generated by vectors of the form $\gamma u_{i}, \gamma \in \Gamma$.

*Here and below $G^{\sigma}$ will denote an algebraic group, defined over $\mathbf{K}^{\sigma}$, which can be obtained by applying $\sigma$ to all the coefficients of the equations defining $G$.

E. B. VINBERG

This will be an I-module of finite type, since it is contained in an I-submodule generated by the vectors $(1/m)u_i$.

$3) \Rightarrow 1)$. Let $|v_j|$ be a system of generatrices of $M$ and let $u_i = (1/m_1)\sum a_{ij}v_j$, $v_j = (1/m_2)\sum b_{ji}u_i$, where $a_{ij}, b_{ji} \in \mathbf{I}$. We can take $\Gamma_0$ in the form of the kernel of the representation of the group $\Gamma$ in the factor module $M/m_1m_2M$.

Remark. If $\mathbf{I}$ is the ring of principal ideals, then the $\mathbf{I}$-module $M$ occurring in property 3 of Lemma 6 must be free. Hence in this case it is possible to find a basis in which all the elements of $\Gamma$ can be expressed by matrices belonging to $M(\mathbf{I})$.

§6. A criterion for determining whether a group generated by reflections is arithmetic

The group $\mathcal{G}$ of motions of Lobachevskii space $\Lambda^n (n\geq 2)$ consists of two connected components, $\mathcal{G}^0$ being a noncompact simple Lie group without center. Let us ascertain which of the discrete groups of motions of $\Lambda^n$ generated by reflections are arithmetic.

First we introduce some notation. If $G$ is an algebraic group, then $\operatorname{Aut} G(\operatorname{Ad} G)$ will denote the group of its automorphisms (inner automorphisms). If $\mathbf{L}$ is a field containing the field $\mathbf{K}$ of definition of the group $G$, then any morphism $\sigma$ of the field $\mathbf{L}$ in $\mathbf{C}$, identical on $\mathbf{K}$, will induce an isomorphism $g \to g^{\sigma}$ of $G_{\mathbf{L}}$ onto $G_{\mathbf{L}^{\sigma}}$. We shall assume that $g^{\sigma r} = (g^{r})^{\sigma}$.

Let $f$ be a quadratic form with coefficients in $\mathbf{K}$. The group of its automorphisms (unimodular automorphisms), as an algebraic group over $\mathbf{K}$, will be denoted by $O(f)(SO(f))$.

The group $\mathcal{G}$ can be identified with the group $(\mathrm{Ad}O(f_0))_{\mathbf{R}} = \mathrm{Ad}O(f_0)_{\mathbf{R}}$, where

$$
f_0 = -x_0^2 + x_1^2 + \dots + x_n^2. \tag{19}
$$

On the other hand, $\mathcal{G}$ can be embedded in the form of a subgroup of index 2 in $O(f_0)_{\mathbf{R}}$.

Lemma 7. Let $\Gamma$ be a Zariski-dense (over $\mathbf{R}$) subgroup of $\mathcal{G}$ containing reflections. Suppose, furthermore, that $G$ is an irreducible algebraic group defined over the real number field $\mathbf{K}$, and that $\phi$ is an isomorphism of $G_{\mathbf{R}}$ on $\mathcal{G}^0$. If $\Gamma \cap \phi(G_{\mathbf{K}})$ is a subgroup of finite index in $\Gamma$, then

1) $G \simeq \operatorname{Ad}SO(f)$, where $f$ is a quadratic form with coefficients in $\mathbf{K}$, and $\phi$ can be (uniquely) extended to an isomorphism of the group $(\operatorname{Ad}O(f))_{\mathbf{R}}$ on $\mathcal{G}$.

2) If $\Gamma$ is generated by reflections, then $\Gamma \subset \phi(\mathrm{Ad}O(f)_{\mathbf{K}})$.

Proof. We shall identify $\mathcal{G}$ with $(\mathrm{Ad}O(f_0))_{\mathbf{R}}$ in such a way that $\phi$ will induce an isomorphism of the algebraic group $G$ on $\mathrm{Ad}SO(f_0)$, defined over a normal extension $\mathbf{L}$ of the field $\mathbf{K}$.

For any $\gamma \in \Gamma$ we have

$$
U_\gamma = \varphi^{-1} \cdot \operatorname{Ad} \gamma \cdot \varphi \in (\operatorname{Aut} G)_{\mathbf{K}}. \tag{20}
$$

In fact, let $U_\gamma \in (\mathrm{Aut}G)_{\mathbf{K}}$, where $\tilde{\mathbf{K}} \supset \mathbf{K}$, and let $\sigma$ be an arbitrary morphism of $\tilde{\mathbf{K}}$ in $\mathbf{C}$, identical on $\mathbf{K}$. Suppose, furthermore, that $\Gamma_0$ is a normal divisor of finite index in $\Gamma$, contained in $\phi(G_{\mathbf{K}})$. The set $\phi^{-1}(\Gamma_0) \subset G_{\mathbf{K}}$ is invariant under $U_\gamma$, and for $g \in \phi^{-1}(\Gamma_0)$ we thus have

$$
U_\gamma^\sigma(g) = U_\gamma^\sigma(g^\sigma) = (U_\gamma(g))^\sigma = U_\gamma(g).
$$

Since $\phi^{-1}(\Gamma_0)$ is Zariski-dense (over $\mathbf{C}$) in the group $G$, it follows that $U_\gamma^\sigma = U_\gamma$.

Let $\Delta = \operatorname{Gal}(\mathbf{L} / \mathbf{K})$. In this case there exist automorphisms $A_\sigma(\sigma \in \Delta)$ of the group $\mathrm{Ad}SO(f_0)$ that are defined over $\mathbf{L}$ and satisfy the relations

DISCRETE GROUPS 439

$$
A_{\sigma\tau} = A_{\sigma} A_{\tau}^{\sigma}, \tag{21}
$$

and are such that

$$
\varphi(G_{\mathbf{K}}) = \{g \in (\operatorname{Ad} SO(f_0)) : A_{\sigma}(g^{\sigma}) = g \ \text{V} \sigma \in \Delta\}.
$$

From (20) it follows that $\operatorname{Ad} \gamma \in (\operatorname{Ad} O(f_0))_{\mathbf{L}}$ and that

$$
A_{\sigma}(\operatorname{Ad} \gamma)^{\sigma} A_{\sigma}^{-1} = \operatorname{Ad} \gamma \quad \text{for} \quad \sigma \in \Delta. \tag{22}
$$

If $\gamma$ is a reflection it follows from (22) that the $A_{\sigma}$ can be extended to automorphisms of the group $\operatorname{Ad} O(f_0)$. It is well known that all the automorphisms of this group are inner automorphisms; therefore $A_{\sigma} \in (\operatorname{Ad} O(f_0))_{\mathbf{L}}$ for all $\sigma \in \Delta$. Hence it is easy to conclude that $A_{\sigma} \in \operatorname{Ad} O(f_0)_{\mathbf{L}}$, where $\mathbf{L}$ is a normal extension of the field $\mathbf{L}$. Since an extension of $\mathbf{L}$ does not cause the appearance of new $A_{\sigma}$, it is possible to assume that $A_{\sigma} \in \operatorname{Ad} O(f_0)_{\mathbf{L}}$. Similarly, for a fixed reflection $\gamma \in \Gamma$ it is possible to assume that $\gamma \in \operatorname{Ad} O(f_0)_{\mathbf{L}}$. Let $A_{\sigma} = \operatorname{Ad} a_{\sigma}$, $\gamma = \operatorname{Ad} r$, where $a_{\sigma}, r \in O(f_0)_{\mathbf{L}}$. We shall consider $a_{\sigma}$ and $r$ as being linear transformations of the $(n+1)$-dimensional vector space $E$, endowed with a quadratic form $f_0$. They are defined to within multiplication by $-1$. The transformation $r$ will be taken in the form of a reflection in a hypersubspace, and $e$ will denote a vector in $E_{\mathbf{L}}$ such that

$$
re = -e, \quad f_0(e) = 1. \tag{23}
$$

(in order to satisfy the second condition we might have to extend the field $\mathbf{L}$).

From (22) it follows that $a_{\sigma} r^{\sigma} a_{\sigma}^{-1} = \pm r$ for $\sigma \in \Delta$; but $\operatorname{Tr} r = \operatorname{Tr} r^{\sigma} = n - 1$, so that

$$
a_{\sigma} r^{\sigma} a_{\sigma}^{-1} = r \quad \text{for} \quad \sigma \in \Delta. \tag{24}
$$

From (21) we get $a_{\sigma \tau} = \pm a_{\sigma} a^{\sigma}$. Let us show that the $a_{\sigma}$ can be selected in such a way that

$$
a_{\sigma\tau} = a_{\sigma} a_{\tau}^{\sigma}. \tag{25}
$$

From (23) and (24) it is easy to see that $a_{\sigma}^{-1} e = \pm e^{\sigma}$. Let us take $a_{\sigma}$ such that $a_{\sigma}^{-1} e = e^{\sigma}$; thus the relation (25) will be satisfied.

In view of (25) the equations $a_{\sigma}(x^{\sigma}) = x (\sigma \in \Delta)$ define a K-form of the space $E$. Let us denote by $f$ the quadratic form induced on the former. Hence $G \simeq \operatorname{Ad} SO(f)$. From (24) it follows that $r \in O(f)_{\mathbf{K}}$. If, therefore, $\Gamma$ is generated by reflections, then $\Gamma \subset \operatorname{Ad} O(f)_{\mathbf{K}}$.

Let us note that if $\sigma$ is a morphism of the field $\mathbf{K}$ in $\mathbf{R}$, then $O(f)^{\sigma} = O(f^{\sigma})$, and for the group $(O(f)^{\sigma})_{\mathbf{R}}$ to be compact it is necessary and sufficient that the quadratic form $f^{\sigma}$ be definite.

We shall now assume that $\mathfrak{G}$ is a group of automorphisms of the pseudo-Euclidean space $E^{n,1}$ that leave a cone $V_{+}$ invariant (see the beginning of $\mathfrak{G}3$). Let $\Gamma$ be a discrete subgroup of $G$ that is generated by reflections and such that the volume of $\mathfrak{G}/\Gamma$ is finite. Lemma 7 shows that the question of whether or not the group $\Gamma$ is quasi-arithmetic reduces to the question of the existence of a completely real field $\mathbf{K}$ and of a basis $|u_i|$ of the space $E^{n,1}$ that have the following properties.

(a) All the transformations in $\Gamma$ can be written in the basis $|u_i|$ with the aid of matrices with elements in $\mathbf{K}$.

(b) $b_{ij} = (u_i, u_j) \in \mathbf{K}$.

(c) The matrix $(b_{ij})$ is definite for any nonidentity morphism $\sigma: \mathbf{K} \to \mathbf{R}$.

For our purposes it is convenient to reformulate these conditions in such a way that no linear

É. B. VINBERG

independence is required of the vectors $u_{i}$. It is evident that this can be done as follows:

(a)' All the transformations in $\Gamma$ leave invariant the K-submodule $E_{\mathbf{K}}$ of the space $E^{n,1}$ generated by the vectors $|u_{i}|$.

(b)' $b_{ij} = (u_i,u_j)\in \mathbf{K}$

(c)' For any nonidentity morphism $\sigma \colon \mathbf{K} \to \mathbf{R}$ the matrix $(b_{ij}^{\sigma})$ is semidefinite.

(From (a)' and (b)' it follows that $\dim_{\mathbf{K}}E_{\mathbf{K}} = n + 1$.)

We shall show that if such a field $\mathbf{K}$ and a K-submodule $E_{\mathbf{K}}$ exist, they will be uniquely determined by the group $\Gamma$ to within multiplication of $E_{\mathbf{K}}$ by a number whose square lies in $\mathbf{K}$. Then the question of whether or not the group $\Gamma$ is arithmetic will be settled with the aid of Lemma 6.

Theorem 2. Let $\Gamma$ be a discrete group of motions of the space $\Lambda^n$ that is generated by finitely many reflections and that has a fundamental polyhedron $P$ of finite volume; let $A = (a_{ij})$ be the Gram matrix of $P$. Denote by $\widehat{\mathbf{K}}$ the field generated by the numbers $a_{ij}$, and by $\mathbf{K}$ the field generated by the numbers

$$
a_{i_1 i_2} a_{i_2 i_3} \dots a_{i_{m-1} i_m} a_{i_m i_1}. \tag{26}
$$

In order that a group $\Gamma$ be quasi-arithmetic it is necessary and sufficient that $\widehat{\mathbf{K}}$ be a completely real field of algebraic numbers and that for any morphism $\sigma \colon \widehat{\mathbf{K}} \to \mathbf{R}$, not identical on $\mathbf{K}$, the matrix $A^{\sigma} = (a_{ij}^{\sigma})$ be nonnegative. In order that a group $\Gamma$ be arithmetic, it is moreover necessary and sufficient that the algebraic numbers $2a_{ij}$ be integers.

Proof. Let $e_i$ be the vectors constructed in §3. The reflections $r_i$ at the faces of $P$ act in $E^{n,1}$ according to the formulas

$$
r_i(x) = x - 2(x, e_i) e_i. \tag{27}
$$

If $T$ is a set in $E^{n,1}$ invariant under $\Gamma$, then $ce_i \in T$ implies that $2ca_{ij}e_j \in T$. Let us introduce the notation

$$
v_{i_1 i_2 \dots i_k} = 2^k a_{1i_1} a_{i_1 i_2} \dots a_{i_{k-1} i_k} e_{i_k}. \tag{28}
$$

It is clear that if $e_1 \in T$, then $v_{i_1 i_2 \dots i_k} \in T$ for any $i_1, i_2, \dots, i_k$.

Now let us assume that there exist a completely real field $\mathbf{K}$ and a K-submodule $E_{\mathbf{K}} \subset E^{n,1}$ that satisfy the conditions (a)'-(c)'. It follows from (27) that $\lambda e_1 \in E_{\mathbf{K}}$ for some nonzero $\lambda$. Since $\lambda^2 = (\lambda e_1, \lambda e_1) \in \mathbf{K}$, it follows that the properties (a)'-(c)' are preserved under multiplication of $E_{\mathbf{K}}$ by $\lambda^{-1}$. Therefore it can be assumed that $e_1 \in E_{\mathbf{K}}$; in this case also $v_{i_1 \dots i_k} \in E_{\mathbf{K}}$.

For every $i$ let us select a chain $i_1, i_2, \dots, i_k$, where $i_k = i$, such that $\lambda_i = 2^k a_{1i_1} a_{i_2 i_3} \dots a_{i_{k-1} i} \neq 0$. This can be done, since the matrix $A$ is nondecomposable (see Theorem 1). The vectors $u_i = v_{i_1 \dots i} = \lambda_i e_i$ generate a K-submodule whose dimensionality is not smaller than $n + 1$. Since this K-submodule is contained in $E_{\mathbf{K}}$ it has dimensionality $n + 1$ and coincides with $E_{\mathbf{K}}$. Let us stipulate that for $i = 1$ we selected a chain of one element $i_1 = 1$; in this case $\lambda_1 = 2$.

Let us form the scalar products of the vectors $u_i$:

$$
b_{ij} = (u_i, u_j) = \lambda_i \lambda_j a_{ij} \in \mathbf{K}. \tag{29}
$$

In particular, $b_{ii} = \lambda_i^2 \in \mathbf{K}$, so that the $\lambda_i$ will be algebraic numbers. Let us denote by $\widehat{\mathbf{K}}$ the field obtained by adjoining these numbers to the field $\mathbf{K}$. It is clear that $a_{ij} \in \widehat{\mathbf{K}}$. Let $\sigma$ be a morphism of

DISCRETE GROUPS

the field $\tilde{\mathbf{K}}$ in C. Then

$$
b_{ij}^{\sigma} = \lambda_i^{\sigma} \lambda_j^{\sigma} a_{ij}^{\sigma}. \tag{30}
$$

If $\sigma$ is not identical on $\mathbf{K}$, then the matrix $(b_{ij}^{\sigma})$ must by definition be semidefinite. Since $b_{11}^{\sigma} = b_{11} = \lambda_1^2 = 4$, it will be nonnegative. We incidentally find that the $\lambda_i$ are completely real numbers. In fact, if $\sigma$ is not identical on $\mathbf{K}$, then $(\lambda_i^{\sigma})^2 = b_{ii}^{\sigma} &gt; 0$; if $\sigma$ is identical on $\mathbf{K}$, then $(\lambda_i^{\sigma})^2 = (\lambda_i^2)^{\sigma} = \lambda_i^2 &gt; 0$. It then follows from (30) that the matrices $(a_{ij}^{\sigma})$ and $(b_{ij}^{\sigma})$ define quadratic forms equivalent over $\mathbf{R}$. Thus we have proved that the field $\tilde{\mathbf{K}}$ is completely real and that for any morphism $\sigma: \tilde{\mathbf{K}} \to \mathbf{R}$, not identical on $\mathbf{K}$, the matrix $A^{\sigma} = (a_{ij}^{\sigma})$ is nonnegative.

Now let us prove that the fields $\mathbf{K}$ and $\tilde{\mathbf{K}}$ coincide with the fields mentioned in the formulation of the theorem. From (29) it follows that

$$
a_{i_1 i_2} a_{i_2 i_3} \dots a_{i_m i_1} = \frac{b_{i_1 i_2} b_{i_3 i_3} \dots b_{i_m i_1}}{b_{i_1 i_1} b_{i_3 i_3} \dots b_{i_m i_m}} \in \mathbf{K},
$$

i.e. the numbers (26) belong to $\mathbf{K}$. Let us note that the principal minors of the matrix $A$ can be expressed in terms of these numbers in the form of polynomials with rational coefficients, and that the inertial indices of a symmetric matrix are fully determined by its principal minors. Hence if the morphism $\sigma: \tilde{\mathbf{K}} \to \mathbf{R}$ is identical on the numbers (26) then the matrix $A^{\sigma}$ cannot be nonnegative, and hence $\sigma$ is identical on $\mathbf{K}$. This means that $\mathbf{K}$ is generated by the numbers (26). It follows directly from this circumstance and from the definition of the numbers $\lambda_i$ that $\tilde{\mathbf{K}}$ is generated by the numbers $a_{ij}$.

Thus we proved the necessity of the quasi-arithmeticity conditions formulated in the theorem. The sufficiency of these conditions can be established by directly verifying that if they are satisfied, then the field $\mathbf{K}$ occurring in the formulation of the theorem, and the $\mathbf{K}$-submodule $E_{\mathbf{K}} \subset E^{n,1}$ generated by vectors of the form (28), will satisfy the conditions $(\mathbf{a})' - (\mathbf{c})'$.

Let us assume that $\Gamma$ is a quasi-arithmetic group. In order to ascertain whether or not it is an arithmetic group, we must (according to Lemma 6) determine whether there exists in $E_{\mathbf{K}}$ an I-submodule $M$ of finite type that is invariant under $\Gamma$. Suppose that such an I-submodule $M$ exists. By multiplying $M$ by an appropriate number $\mu \in \mathbf{K}$, we can achieve that $e_1 \in M$. In this case all the vectors (28) will also belong to $M$. Let us set $\alpha = (2a_{ij})^2 = 4a_{ij}a_{ji}$. For any natural $s$ the vector $2a_{1i}\alpha^s v_i$ has the form (28), and hence it belongs to $M$. Therefore the vectors $2a_{1i}\alpha^s v_i$ generate an I-submodule of finite type; but this is possible only if $\alpha \in \mathbf{I}$, i.e. if $2a_{ij}$ is an integer.

Conversely, if we know that all the numbers $2a_{ij}$ are integers, then the numbers $2^m a_{i_1 i_2} a_{i_2 i_3} \dots a_{i_m i_1}$ are also integers, which means that they belong to $\mathbf{I}$. It is easy to verify that an $\mathbf{I}$-submodule $M$, generated by all the vectors (28) and evidently invariant under $\Gamma$, has finitely many generatrices. In fact, such generatrices can be taken in the form of vectors (28) with distinct subscripts.

This completes the proof of the theorem.

Remarks. 1. If the fundamental polyhedron $P$ of the group $\Gamma$ is noncompact, the formulation of Theorem 2 can be greatly simplified. Indeed, in this case the necessary and sufficient condition for a group $\Gamma$ to be quasi-arithmetic is that the numbers (26) be rational.

For the proof let us consider the principal $C^0$-submatrix $B$ of $A$, which corresponds to some infinitely distant vertex of $P$. Its rows are linearly dependent, but the rows of the matrix $A$ which pass through it are linearly independent. This property is preserved under any morphism $\sigma: \tilde{\mathbf{K}} \to \mathbf{R}$.

E. B. VINBERG

On the other hand it cannot hold for a nonnegative matrix. Hence for a group $\Gamma$ to be quasi-arithmetic, it is necessary that $\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{Q}$.

2. It is easy to verify that the principal $C^+$-submatrices of $A$ remain positive under any morphism $\sigma: \tilde{\mathbf{K}} \to \mathbf{R}$. Therefore if we denote by $D$ the determinant of any principal submatrix of order $n + 1$ adjacent to a principal $C^+$-submatrix of order $n$, the condition $A^\sigma \geq 0$ will be equivalent to the condition $D^\sigma &gt; 0$. Since $D \in \mathbf{K}$ and $D &lt; 0$, the quasi-arithmeticity condition can be satisfied only if $D$ is a primitive element of the field $\mathbf{K}$.

Hence the quasi-arithmeticity criterion can be reformulated as follows: The number $D$ must be a primitive element of the field $\mathbf{K}$, and all its conjugate numbers must be positive.

3. If no dotted lines occur in Coxeter's diagram of the group $\Gamma$, i.e. all the $a_{ij} \geq -1$ ($i \neq j$), then the numbers $2a_{ij}$ will all be integers. Hence in this case the fact that a group $\Gamma$ is quasi-arithmetic implies that it is arithmetic. In general this is not true, as will be shown by the examples below.

## III. EXAMPLES

In this part we shall consider only discrete groups $\Gamma$ in a space $\Lambda^n$ that are generated by finitely many reflections and have a fundamental polyhedron $P$ of finite volume. No proofs will be presented, since by virtue of Theorems 1 and 2 these proofs reduce to elementary (and easy) calculations.

1. Groups $\Gamma$ whose fundamental polyhedra are simplexes. Such groups are easiest to construct: it is merely necessary to draw any connected diagram that has the following properties.

1) The number of vertices is $n + 1$.

2) The diagram is not contained in Coxeter's tables (presented in $\frac{\sigma}{2}4$).

3) Any subdiagram of $n$ vertices either is a combination of several diagrams from Coxeter's first table, or is contained in Coxeter's second table.

To subdiagrams of the first type (Condition 3) there correspond ordinary vertices of the simplex $P$, and to subdiagrams of the second type correspond infinitely distant vertices.

Groups of this kind, for which the simplex $P$ is bounded, were obtained for the first time by Lanner $[\mathbf{3}]$ from a combinatorial analysis. They exist only for $n \leq 4$. In $\Lambda^3$ there are 9 such groups, and in $\Lambda^4$ there are 5 such groups. For $n &gt; 2$ these groups contain precisely one which is nonarithmetic:

$$
\boxed{\begin{array}{c}\end{array}}
$$

(for it we have $\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{5})$).

There are likewise only a few groups $\Gamma$ with an unbounded simplex as the fundamental region. They exist only for $n \leq 9$. For $n &gt; 2$, such groups contain precisely 7 which are nonarithmetic: 6 in $\Lambda^3$ and one in $\Lambda^5$. The diagrams of two of these groups are as follows:

$$
\boxed{\begin{array}{c}\end{array}}
$$

(in both cases we have $\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{Q}(\sqrt{2})$).

2. Some arithmetic groups. For $n \leq 9$ the group $\Gamma_n$ of integral automorphisms of the quadratic

DISCRETE GROUPS

form $f_0 = -x_0^2 + x_1^2 + \cdots + x_n^2$ is generated by reflections at the faces of the simplex. The diagrams of these groups are as follows:

It would be interesting to know whether the group $\Gamma_{n}$ contains a subgroup of finite index, generated by reflections, for all $n$. The author has been able to prove this for $n \leq 16$.

3. Makarov groups. The first example of a nonarithmetic discrete group with a fundamental region of finite volume in a symmetric space different from $\Lambda^2$ was constructed by Makarov [5]. He considered groups generated by reflections at the faces of a polyhedron $P \subset \Lambda^3$ in the form of a combinatorial type of triangular prism and represented by the diagram

$$
\Gamma_{m}^{\prime} \begin{array}{c} C \\ \bullet \end{array} \begin{array}{c} \text{一} m \\ \bullet \end{array} \begin{array}{c} \text{一} m \\ \bullet \end{array} (m \geqslant 5, \varepsilon = \frac{\cos \frac{\pi}{24}}{\sqrt{\cos \frac{2\pi}{24}}})
$$

It is shown in [5] that for a sufficiently large $m$ such a group is not arithmetical.

With the aid of Theorem 2 it can be established that the group $\Gamma_{m}^{\prime}$ is not quasi-arithmetic for any $m \neq 6$.

Similar, though bounded, polyhedra in $\Lambda^3$ were considered by Makarov in [4] (where the question of whether or not a group is arithmetic was not posed). The diagram of one series of such polyhedra is as follows:

$$
\Gamma_{m}^{\prime\prime} \begin{array}{c} \text{一} \varepsilon \\ \bullet \end{array} \begin{array}{c} \text{一} \sigma \\ \bullet \end{array} \begin{array}{c} \text{一} \sigma \\ \bullet \end{array} (m \geqslant 7, \delta = \sqrt{\frac{J \cos \frac{2\pi}{24} - 1}{4 \cos \frac{2\pi}{24} - 2}})
$$

The corresponding group $\Gamma_{m}^{\prime\prime}$ is arithmetic for $m = 7, 8, 9, 10$ and 14; quasi-arithmetic, but not arithmetic, for $m = 12, 18, 24$ and 30; not quasi-arithmetic for all other $m$.

1. As J.-P. Serre has kindly pointed out to the author, the definition given in §5 for an arithmetical discrete subgroup is not sufficiently broad. For if the group $\mathcal{G}$ admits an invariant complex structure, i.e. if it is a complex Lie group, then the following method of constructing discrete subgroups of $\mathcal{G}$ is also possible.

Let $G$ be an irreducible algebraic group defined over an imaginary field $\mathbf{K}$ of algebraic numbers. We assume that the following conditions hold.

(CA1) All fields conjugate to $\mathbf{K}$, except for $\mathbf{K}$ itself and its complex conjugate, are real.

(CA2) The group $G_{\mathbf{C}}$ is locally isomorphic to $\mathcal{G}$.

(CA3) For an arbitrary morphism $b: \mathbf{K} \to \mathbf{R}$ the group $(G^{b})_{\mathbb{R}}$ is compact.

Let us take any exact matrix representation $\rho$ of the group $G$ and set $G_{\mathbf{I}} = \{g \in G_{\mathbf{C}} : \rho(g)_{ij} \in \mathbf{I}\}$, where $\mathbf{I}$ is the ring of integral elements of $\mathbf{K}$. The group $G_{\mathbf{I}}$ is independent, up to commensurability, of $\rho$. If $\phi$ is a homomorphism of $G_{\mathbf{C}}$ onto $\mathcal{G}^0$, then the subgroup $\Gamma = \phi(G_{\mathbf{I}})$ of $\mathcal{G}$ is discrete and the volume of the factor space $\mathcal{G}/\Gamma$ is finite. The subgroups $\Gamma$ of $\mathcal{G}$ obtained in this way, and also the subgroups commensurate with them, will be called complex-arithmetical, and in contrast to them the subgroups obtained by the construction in §5 (if $\mathcal{G}$ is a real Lie group) will be called real-arithmetical.

The group of motions of the space $\Lambda^n$ admits a complex structure only for $n = 3$. The author does not know precisely which of the discrete groups in $\Lambda^3$ constructed in the present article are complex-arithmetical. But in any case it is necessary for this property that the numbers $2a_{ij}$ be integers. Moreover, it is easy to show that for an unbounded fundamental domain complex-arithmeticity implies real-arithmeticity.

2. E. M. Andreev has shown that a bounded convex polyhedron in the space $\Lambda^n$, $n \geq 3$, with dihedral angles not exceeding $90^\circ$, is uniquely defined by its dihedral angles. It follows that a discrete group generated by reflections in $\Lambda^n$, $n \geq 3$, is completely described, in the case of a bounded fundamental domain, by its scheme, without indication of the numbers $a_{ij}$ corresponding to broken lines. It remains an open question whether this statement holds for unbounded fundamental domains.
